source.title: Beyond Scale: the Diversity Coefficient as a Data Quality Metric Demonstrates LLMs are Pre-trained on Formally Diverse Data
source.authors: Brando Miranda; Alycia Lee; S. Sundar; Allison Casasola; Rylan Schaeffer; Elyas Obbad; Sanmi Koyejo

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper cites scaling-law work and frames its contribution as going beyond scale, but it does not test or rely on the claim’s scaling relationships, extrapolations, compute-optimal allocations, architecture sensitivity, or fit dependence.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that changing pre-training data diversity changes validation cross-entropy. Those results concern data quality, not whether loss follows the specified scaling laws or is predictable from scale or pre-training loss. They are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version; no claim version is tested.
record.test_reason: The paper cites scaling-law work (Kaplan, Hoffmann) only to motivate going beyond scale. Its experiments vary pre-training data diversity at a fixed token count within each experiment. Model size and token count co-vary irregularly across experiments: 51M on 550M tokens, 1.5B on 180M, 7B on 6.36M. No loss-versus-scale sweep, extrapolation, compute-optimal search, shape ablation or exponent fit is reported, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, with one correction. The abstract and introduction state that higher-diversity pre-training data causally leads to better evaluation performance (lower validation cross-entropy), across GPT-2 and LLaMA2 models from 51M to 7B. Only the Discussion appendix calls the performance evidence preliminary and says more extensive experiments are needed. The authors also conclude the diversity coefficient is a trustworthy metric and that public pre-training corpora are formally highly diverse.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures data diversity with Task2Vec and intervenes on pre-training data composition; it does not reproduce a scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported diversity-coefficient value changes with batch size and probe-network configuration: larger batches increase the coefficient with diminishing returns; random probe networks tend to underestimate it, and non-fine-tuned pretrained networks overestimate it relative to fine-tuned pretrained networks.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed tokens and hyperparameters within each experiment, validation cross-entropy on OpenWebText2/C4 is lower for pre-training on more diverse data (USPTO 0.158 < PubMed 0.168 < USPTO+PubMed 0.195). The text says this holds across 15 runs, with average R² of about 0.79–0.82.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-training data diversity (Task2Vec diversity coefficient) affects held-out loss independently of scale.

record.problems: The downstream-loss evidence is described by the authors as preliminary, and the paper says more extensive experiments are needed. The Figure 2 loss values are not given in the text. Some detailed entries in Tables 3 and 4 are flattened, so individual model-to-value mappings are unclear.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed numeric results in Tables 3 and 4 were not separately extracted because the flattened table layout does not reliably map all values to their model, training-data condition, and evaluation dataset. The reported aggregate trend across 15 runs is captured in r4.

untested.parts: No loss vs parameters/tokens/compute power-law sweep; sizes and tokens co-vary across experiments.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.
No scaling-law form tested in other modalities or regimes.
Validation loss is not related to scale or pretraining loss; only to data diversity.
No exponent fitting or fit-choice analysis.

record.verdict_notes: The relation could arguably be 'discusses', since the framing is 'beyond scale'. However, no specific argument is made that any version is wrong. Tables 3/4 give losses at several model sizes, but token counts and datasets vary non-systematically, so they cannot be read as a scaling test.

versions.untested_parts: No loss-versus-parameter, token, or compute scaling sweep.
No extrapolation from small runs to larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for optimal parameter and token allocations.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No test of scaling-law form across modalities or other training regimes.
The study measures downstream validation loss after changing pre-training data diversity, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from model scale or pre-training loss.
No analysis of scaling-law exponents, fitting choices, or departures from power-law curves.

rows.subject: GPT2-51M
rows.operation_detail: Pre-trained on USPTO data for 1.31 B tokens with other hyperparameters held identical across the compared runs.
rows.note: The paper compares this result with the PubMed and USPTO + PubMed training-data runs; loss decreases as the reported training-data diversity increases.
rows.check: Bears on no version, so a version state cannot apply. Table 2's caption says 51.5M parameters and 1.31B tokens. That conflicts with Section 3.1 (51M trained on 550M tokens) and Table 4 (GPT2-51M at 328M/550M tokens, GPT2-204M at 1.31B). The subject or token count may be mislabelled.

rows.subject: GPT2-51M
rows.operation_detail: Pre-trained on PubMed data for 1.31 B tokens with other hyperparameters held identical across the compared runs.
rows.note: The loss is slightly lower than for USPTO training, while the reported diversity coefficient is higher.
rows.check: Bears on no version. 'partial' is not meaningful without a linked version. The value 6.4204 vs 6.4414 is read correctly from Table 2. The same subject/token inconsistency as r1 applies.

rows.subject: GPT2-51M
rows.operation_detail: Pre-trained on an equal mixture of USPTO and PubMed data for 1.31 B tokens with other hyperparameters held identical across the compared runs.
rows.note: This run has the highest reported training-data diversity and lowest loss among the three Table 2 runs.
rows.check: Bears on no version. The value 6.1815 is read correctly. The same subject/token inconsistency as r1 applies.

rows.subject: 15 GPT-2 and LLaMA2 runs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared runs trained on datasets with increasing diversity coefficients while controlling token count and other hyperparameters within each experiment.
rows.value: The paper states that loss falls on all 15 runs as training-data diversity increases; numeric values are figure-only.
rows.note: Aggregate statement across the reported runs; this is an effect of data-diversity interventions, not a scaling-law test.
rows.check: Bears on no version; this is a data-diversity effect. The run count is ambiguous: the abstract says 44 models, Section 3.1 says 15 runs.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
